speaker: Chris Young
title: A Conversation With Chef Chris Young
question: In home kitchens, why has voice control failed to take off despite being a natural hands-free interface for messy cooking?
guest: When you're a professional chef, a lot of how you make things happen in your kitchen is by communicating your intent to your sous chefs and chef de parties. So to me, it always made sense that when your hands are covered in goop, a voice interface is great. There have been a lot of problems making that happen, and a big part of it is Amazon and Google can do all the work they want on making those technologies better at understanding your intent, but if the appliances they're connected to are too stupid to know how to respond to that information, then it's not going to go anywhere. Right now, most of the major companies making appliances don't know how to think about a future where their devices are smarter and leverage software to allow humans to be more creative. Unlike a pure software company, if you're selling physical hardware for the kitchen, you have to deal with atoms, and there are very few companies able to think cohesively about both bending metal and software interfaces that keep humans at the center of the kitchen.

points.core: The bottleneck is dumb kitchen appliances unable to act on spoken intent.
points.note: Accept: voice recognition works well enough, but connected appliances lack the intelligence or actuation capabilities to respond meaningfully to commands. Do not credit: blaming speech recognition accuracy alone.

points.core: Legacy appliance makers excel at physical manufacturing rather than software-driven user experiences.
points.note: Accept: traditional manufacturers focus on hardware and metal-bending and struggle to conceive software-augmented cooking tools. Do not credit: generic claims that big companies are slow to innovate.

points.core: Very few teams combine physical hardware engineering with human-centered interface design.
points.note: Accept: scarcity of organizations able to integrate physical manufacturing (atoms) with software interfaces that keep cooks in creative control. Do not credit: vague calls for better UX.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Voice control in kitchens has stalled mostly because it's unreliable exactly where it's needed, and it solves too small a problem to justify its friction.

Kitchens are acoustically hostile: range hoods, running water, sizzling pans, dishwashers and conversation all degrade speech recognition, so commands fail or need repeating, which is more annoying than wiping a hand and tapping a button. Cooking also depends on visual, glanceable information. Recipes involve ingredient lists, quantities and steps you want to scan and revisit, and voice is serial and ephemeral, forcing you to remember what was said or ask again.

In practice, usage has collapsed to a few trivial tasks: setting timers, converting units, playing music. Those work well, but they don't make appliance voice control worth paying for. Controlling ovens or cooktops by voice adds safety concerns, clumsy setup, fragmented ecosystems and rigid command phrasing, while a physical knob is faster and more trustworthy.

Privacy unease about always-on microphones and the weak business case for assistants (Amazon lost billions on Alexa) further dampened investment. Newer LLM-based assistants may improve the conversation, but noise and the need for visuals remain.

points.why: The response blames speech recognition failures and control friction without identifying appliances’ limited ability to act on understood commands.
The response omits how traditional appliance makers’ strengths in physical manufacturing leave them ill-equipped to design software-driven cooking experiences.
The response discusses interface drawbacks but never identifies the scarcity of teams that combine appliance engineering with software design that keeps cooks in creative control.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Voice control has stalled in kitchens because the acoustic environment, cooking workflows, and safety regulations all work against it. Kitchens are loud—range hoods, sizzling pans, running water, and blenders drown out microphones right when urgency peaks, making it faster to nudge a knob with a clean knuckle or elbow than to repeat a misheard command. Voice also clashes with how people cook: managing heat demands instant, continuous micro-adjustments rather than rigid spoken syntax, and following recipes relies on quick visual scanning rather than slow, linear audio readouts that tax divided attention. Worse, safety standards like UL 858 and IEC 60335 classify voice as remote operation, requiring users to physically press an enable button on ovens or cooktops before spoken commands can activate heating elements—defeating the hands-free premise. Combined with decade-long appliance replacement cycles and fragmented, cloud-dependent apps, kitchen voice control remains largely confined to low-stakes tasks like setting timers and playing music.

points.why: The response attributes limited command execution to misheard speech and safety requirements without identifying a lack of appliance intelligence or actuation capability.

The response mentions long replacement cycles and fragmented apps without connecting those issues to legacy manufacturers’ hardware expertise or difficulty designing software-driven cooking experiences.

The response describes friction between voice commands and cooking workflows without identifying a shortage of teams that can integrate appliance engineering with interfaces that keep cooks in control.

noweb.answer:
Voice control struggles in home kitchens because the environment and mechanics of cooking work directly against speech interfaces. Acoustically, kitchens are hostile: sizzling pans, roaring range hoods, running faucets, and blenders routinely drown out wake words and garble commands right when a cook needs immediate action. 

Even in a quiet room, voice is too slow and imprecise for active cooking. Twisting a knob to stop a pot from boiling over takes a split second and gives instant tactile feedback, whereas speaking a structured command and waiting for cloud processing introduces clumsy latency—especially for continuous adjustments like "a little lower." Safety rules further hollow out the hands-free promise: to prevent fires and injuries, manufacturers and regulators typically require a physical button press on the appliance before heating elements or blades can activate, making subsequent voice triggers redundant. Combined with decade-long appliance replacement cycles and fragmented smart-home ecosystems, voice has largely stalled at ambient tasks like setting timers or converting units on a countertop speaker rather than actually operating the kitchen.

points.why: The response attributes limited appliance control to speech interference, latency, safety interlocks, and ecosystem fragmentation, leaving appliance intelligence unaddressed.
The response mentions manufacturers in connection with safety rules and leaves their manufacturing strengths and software design capabilities unaddressed.
The response compares voice commands with tactile controls and leaves unaddressed the scarcity of teams that can integrate hardware engineering with interfaces that keep cooks in control.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Voice control did succeed in the kitchen for a few simple jobs. Setting timers, converting units and adding items to a shopping list are among the most common smart-speaker uses. What never caught on is using voice to actually run the cooking, for several reasons.

Kitchens are hard on speech recognition. Range hoods, running water, sizzling pans and clattering dishes cause misheard commands, and a mistake costs more when food is burning. Cooking also depends on continuous, by-feel adjustments like "a bit lower" or "just until golden." A knob handles those instantly and silently. Discrete spoken commands with a wake word and a short delay don't.

Appliance control is fragmented across brands, apps and ecosystems, so setup is a chore for little benefit. Safety rules and liability concerns also limit what can be started remotely, especially burners. Reading a recipe aloud sounds useful, but moving through one ("go back," "how much flour again?") was clumsy with older assistants, and the answers are hard to remember without seeing them, so people prop up a phone or tablet instead. Privacy worries about always-listening microphones and the lack of investment in assistants like Alexa slowed things further. Newer AI models may improve the conversation, but noise, the need for fine control and the setup hassle remain.

points.why: The response cites fragmented controls, safety restrictions, and limits of spoken commands without identifying appliances’ inability to interpret and act on spoken intent as the bottleneck.
The response does not connect legacy manufacturers’ strength in physical production to difficulty designing software-driven cooking experiences.
The response describes usability problems without identifying a scarcity of teams that combine hardware engineering with interface design that keeps cooks in creative control.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Voice control sounds ideal for messy cooking, but home kitchens are hostile environments for it. Range hoods, sizzling pans, blenders, and running water create constant background noise that makes wake words unreliable and forces cooks to shout or repeat commands—often just as something is about to burn. Even when voice recognition works, audio is a poor medium for recipes: cooks want to skim ingredients, jump between steps, and check quantities at a glance, whereas linear spoken instructions are slow and frustrating to navigate. Meanwhile, most kitchen actions still require physical presence—stirring, opening doors, or checking doneness—so hands-free control rarely saves real effort over turning a dial or tapping a screen. Safety concerns also limit voice control of heat-generating appliances, while speaking commands aloud in a shared space feels socially awkward and interrupts music or conversation. Outside simple timers and unit conversions, voice adds more friction than it removes.

The response does not connect legacy appliance makers’ expertise in physical manufacturing to difficulty designing software-driven cooking experiences.
The response describes interface friction without identifying a shortage of teams that can integrate appliance engineering with software that keeps cooks in creative control.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Voice control solves the problem of messy hands, but cooking also demands quick, reliable feedback. A running tap, extractor fan, or blender can make a command harder to hear. If you have to repeat yourself or check whether the oven actually changed temperature, turning a knob is often faster. A display also lets you scan several timers, compare quantities, or see where you are in a recipe at a glance. Spoken instructions arrive one step at a time and can be awkward to revisit.

Setup and compatibility add friction, especially when appliances from different brands support different commands. And the cost of a missed command matters more when it controls heat than when it plays a song. That’s why voice has found a foothold in short, easy-to-confirm tasks like setting a timer or converting measurements, while buttons, knobs, and screens still do most of the work.

points.why: The response cites missed commands, uncertain feedback, and compatibility friction without identifying appliances’ inability to act on correctly understood intent as the bottleneck.
The response notes differences in command support across brands without linking them to legacy manufacturers’ hardware expertise or difficulty designing software-driven cooking tools.
The response compares interface tradeoffs without identifying the scarcity of teams that combine physical appliance engineering with software design that keeps cooks in control.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Messy hands make voice control appealing, but only for certain tasks. “Set a timer for ten minutes” is easy to say, and a beep tells you it worked. Turning down a burner is usually quicker with a knob, especially when you’re already standing at the stove and can see the flame change.

Voice also has to work when the extractor fan is running, water is flowing, and people are talking. Repeating a command breaks the flow of cooking. Checking whether the oven heard the right temperature takes away much of the hands-free benefit. And while a screen or recipe card lets you glance back at a quantity while you stir, a spoken instruction has to be replayed. That’s why voice has found a place in kitchens for timers, music, and quick conversions, while everyday appliance controls have largely stayed physical.
